props.title: Cadillac Records

sections.content: Cadillac Records (2008) captures the electrifying rise of Chess Records, the legendary Chicago blues label that helped birth rock 'n' roll. Adrien Brody portrays Leonard Chess, who recorded pioneers like Muddy Waters and Chuck Berry, while Jeffrey Wright delivers a haunting performance as Waters. The film joins other powerful music biopics like Ray (2004) and Walk the Line (2005) in exploring how Black musicians shaped American popular music while facing systemic racism. Director Darnell Martin unflinchingly shows both the creative triumphs and personal struggles, particularly through Beyoncé's raw portrayal of Etta James.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in showing how Chess Records captured the Great Migration's impact on American music. Like Dreamgirls (2006) and What's Love Got to Do with It (1993), it reveals the exploitation many Black artists faced from white-owned record labels. The movie particularly shines in its concert sequences, with Jeffrey Wright and Mos Def (as Chuck Berry) performing their own vocals, adding authenticity rarely seen in music biopics like Jersey Boys (2014).

While some critics noted historical inaccuracies, Cadillac Records succeeds in capturing the raw energy of Chicago blues and early rock 'n' roll. The film shares DNA with Twenty Feet from Stardom (2013) in highlighting overlooked musical pioneers. Columbus Short's portrayal of Little Walter shows the tragic toll of fame, while Cedric the Entertainer brings comic relief as Willie Dixon, the songwriter behind many blues standards. sections.content: Cadillac Records represents a shift from sanitized music biopics like The Glenn Miller Story (1954) toward grittier portraits like Love & Mercy (2014) about Beach Boys' Brian Wilson. The film's ensemble approach influenced later works like Straight Outta Compton (2015), showing how musical movements emerge from specific cultural moments and places.
